Just yesterday, I would have believed you. But with everything that's changed—Hamlet might very well come out of this a new young man.
A-ah—it must be because of—well, I heard the story about what happened with your father.
But a spirit— a vision, is something else entirely. You could have my reputation shattered. And my uncle would be all too gleeful over it.
If you are interested in seeing me perform something special—maybe based upon some juicy gossip—feel free to let me know!
(Well, it's Brit—or was— but I'll feign ignorance.)
They—they did?
And—with young Laertes gone, I expect your heart is heavy right now.
Yes. In a way, it is peaceful.
All suffering is, in one way or another, caused by death, or the fear of it...
Now that fear is removed forever, replaced by an equally-deep boredom.
Even still, this boredom is refreshing at the moment, though I anticipate it, too, will grow old.
And when it does... well.
To divest oneself of the fear of death, one need only give into it.
How does one divest oneself of eternal boredom?
Indeed. A most frightening prospect.
Yes. As we've discussed before, it has never been a concern of mine.
It does not.
I made my peace with it long before my death.
Though they were only one in body near the end of my life... their feelings for one another extended to far before that.
Something in Gerta and I died far sooner, when the others did.
Ah. It would not be common knowledge for anyone other than Irma and Gerta, I expect.
Hamlet was our first living child. But Gerta was with child before that. Four times in all.
The first she lost very near to birth. We thought the child might live, but we were wrong.
The second and third emerged simply as a stream of blood.
She saw each loss as a failure unto herself.
After we lost our third child, I no longer knew what to say to her, and she to me.
If she could not give me an heir, she could not fulfill her duties as Queen, as she saw them. And to her, that was the gravest failing of all.
When she was with child a fourth time, she had already picked out a place to bury him in the graveyard, so certain was she that he would die.
But Hamlet lived. And our miracle son was born.
Claudius knew nothing of the lost children, as far as I know. He was a comfort to her. He was warm and gentle to her in ways I was not.
Over time that comfort grew to familiarity, then to affection, then to love. I witnessed it and I did not stop it.
My wife has suffered enough in this life. Improper though it may be for a man to allow his wife to be wooed by his brother...
If it would purchase her one single shred of happiness, I would overlook nearly anything in the world for Gerta.
I—I had no idea. My sincerest apologies for prying, King Hamlet.
Gertrude? I—I don't know quite what to say about that.
Certainly. You're in luck—Bernardo ordered me to turn over the key, but he hasn't come for it yet.
My apologies. It's just—
This card game you mentioned—it's unpopular with the others?
Before the slippers she wore to his funeral had even been broken in—a funeral where she followed his body like Niobe, all tears—
It's too late for me to do something public about this—expose them for who they are, on stage...
All the things I did for her—
Otherwise, if I start to think about it—
In the past, I would have turned to Brit for something like this. But—well.
It's too late for me to do something public about this—to expose them for who they are, on stage...
He asked me to watch Claudius closely for any hint of—well, guilt, I suppose.
He had asked me to watch Claudius closely for any hint of—well, guilt, I suppose.
But those beady little eyes of his—who knows what horrors he's capable of!
I showed the very location to his men not long after he spoke with you. My mother—was in shock. I couldn't leave him there with her.
And—he was right.
Rest assured—he will be dealt with in swift time.
I warned him to stay his hand, but he listened not.
Grow used to the sting of loss, Ophelia. You will see it yet many hundreds of times before you are free.
I can't speak about this right now, my lady. Apologies for being evasive, but—many things have taken place in the last few hours.
Had Hamlet been... properly disciplined before now—had someone intervened—your father might yet live.
I knew she was unhappy. But to this extent—to the point of treason? How can it be?
That's not what I was aski—you know what, forget I said anything.
Still, to lose one's life so young—it is a shame.
You're going to continue meeting with him until he has all the information he needs to overtake Elsinore. And then, Brit—then everyone will die.
Those eyes will watch for any opportune moment—and then they'll find him and release him back to his men.
Look, Ophelia—a little free advice between friends...
There are gaps in my knowledge between my death and my... awakening.
I know not where they live now. Only that he has certainly taken them from where they once lay.
I can feel the cobwebs of my memory being dusted away gently.
Ah, to be alive, to remember... my utter failure.
That book... I gave up in the end, didn't I? And I let... that cursed thing win, break me down...
Yes. Like you, I was doomed to repeat the occasion of my death. Hundreds of times. Thousands.
And like you, the timeline of my death was no more than a week. My son Hamlet was away at Wittenberg, my brother Claudius plotting to take my throne.
How long was I trapped in that insane void between life and death? Centuries? Millennia? I know not...
It was peaceful to forget for a while, but even now, I cannot be truly dead. No, here I am, still animated, grimacing, like a starved dog brought back to life, forced to bare my teeth...
I cannot truly rest until my brother pays for his crime, the crime I spent a thousand years trying to avoid!
A way out!
A choice between versions of a private hell!
But I was not permitted that much! No, I had to give up! I lay there in the garden, being poisoned by my own brother over and over again, for years before I was freed!
I scoured every inch of the castle, every nook and flagstone and drawer—it isn't here, Ophelia! It simply isn't!
Why did I have to give up, to expire into madness alone?
Ophelia! Find the book! Find the book and save your own soul!
You know that name? How? How can you know?
It is eternally more worthwhile to fight than to give up as I did, Ophelia. Never forget that. For you, hope lingers.
I believe that you will live to see winter come to Denmark—putting an end to this cursed summer.
Perhaps it is too late, after all.
Insanity—death—they have always plagued our family. My mother Astrid was no exception.
I often wonder if she died like me, if she saw time repeating itself. I cannot bear to think of her suffering the same pain I did.
Impossible to tell. My mother is long dead.
Yes. The Book of Fates. I remember our discussion.
Is there some unfinished buisness holding you back from making a choice?
Do not turn away from this oppertunity, Ophelia.
If only Astrid was still alive, or haunted these walls as I, we could ask her.
I told him I wanted to learn from the Book, to learn to be like him. He indulged me by granting it to me once more—of course he did.
I just wanted to find a way to save them all—and myself.
It wasn't spoken of in my lifetime.
Even Claudius and I have never passed her name between us. She... my mother...
Terrible, bloody deeds were committed. My father was a cruel and greedy man.
I do not know her whereabouts, but if she left Elsinore, she must have passed through town.
But I am confined to these walls. I may not leave the board's edges.
Then you know only one small piece of it.
I have suffered far more than anyone, even you, can understand.
Perhaps one year, one century from now—then you may come to comprehend.
You should know by now. Those are the events that were meant to come to pass.
That is the tragic fate which is written before you. For mine own self, it was my poisoning.
To think you can find a future where that does not happen is futile. Give up the sooner and you will drift into endless sleep.
And it's said he discarded her in favor of younger women quite often—a womanizer who could not be satiated!
She passed when Claudius and I were both children.
Evidently, she died of childbirth with my brother. One more life he's ruined in this world, I expect.
It matters not. My father loved her, at least in front of the court, and I remember her very little.
Come to think of it, your father and your mother were both ardently devoted to her.
Death is a wall. Very little permeates it.
I am ashamed.
But I cannot hide the truth.
All I can do is offer my deepest apologies. My decision was clearly in error.
Polonius and I never spoke of it at the time, but...
I would understand if you no longer spoke to me.
In that case, I am at your service.
Nothing I could say could possible amend that crime.
So I will say nothing more.
The... details are indescribably hazy. It is hard to remember.
But I recall he was kind to me. Kinder than I deserved, considering I was not able to help him.
Of course. Now I now he was just using me for his own ends.
We must stop him, Ophelia. There are no limits to what that man will do.
...It was a pressing request of his—something I could not... find...
My memories drift away like fog. Retrieve my final writings from your father. Perhaps then we can make sense of this nothingness.
To help him find the Book of Fates... the token which created this sad situation.
I was never able to find it, of course... but even knowing gave me purpose.
The will to try again indefinitely. The will to return, even now.
Hamlet—and I—we spoke honestly. For perhaps the first time in our lives.
Hamlet—your uncle is not your enemy. Peter Quince is.
I know the one you mean, I think, though it's been years. I—I see. So you believe he's trying to hurt someone?
I met Simona, and she revealed to me the true culprit—Peter Quince, the playmaster, is behind us being trapped in Elsinore.
Yes. Hamlet, you, and I shall act anon.
A ghost, a mad prince, and... you. What a trio we shall be.
Peter Quince? He is but flesh and blood. What ill can he do to you?
No. Impossible. Quince encouraged me to find the Book of Fates.
He urged me to find a way out using the Book as my guide...
For what purpose could he desire such an artifact?
Because he's trapped in this world—our world—until I use the Book of Fates and free us both. That's why he's been in Elsinore for so long.
Boredom can be quite frightening. Even I, who have been dead but a scarce several months, understand how frightening it is.
Unable to truly die, yet unable to engage with human life...
It is like standing outside a window, watching those inside gorge themselves on a feast. I press my hands against the glass nightly.
But try as I might, I cannot join them. I have relinquished my seat at that table, and a wolf now sits in my place.
Here I remain, bored out of my bones, lingering like refuse.
Yes. Cruelty is one cure for that boredom. A route I myself was inspired to take. And now my son wages revenge on my behalf.
Agreed. You must bring my son to me.
Yes—bring him here with those same words, and the three of us shall conspire to end Quince.
I did not understand when you brought him to me in this world. But now I do. Try once more, Ophelia.
I am aware.
He must be dealt with. But we cannot let him know of our plans.
You—you did?
After so many years with Hamlet—he was so terribly cold to her.
Yes. We're addressing it anon. The King is aware—fear not.
I do, but—I also think those notes contain something important.
If you were to describe what you saw to the wrong people, it would put Father—and both of us—in grave danger.
Well, Bernardo—or Katherine—is more than a little tormented over others finding out about this.
Very funny. But truly—have you seen anything... suspicious?
I—I don't think this is the kind of help they mean.
Since you know the truth about me—No. Not a chance. Who told you that rubbish?
But no—I don't believe that for an instant. Claudius is far too dull to play chess like that.
No, 'Feely, I have—had, at least—a special monopoly on wanting you dead.
Ophelia? Did—did you do that?
Oy! I-is—wos that—what just—Ophelia?
It's almost like a little game. Watch them run, seek them out—
Or—perhaps this is merely a tool I can use to amuse myself.
I don't know what you are—spirit or demon or otherwise. But no justice could apply to you.
But someday, you'll be just like me, too. And then—you'll know.
Or—well—how many times have you used that gift now? Been quite a few, hasn't it?
Die, then—whoever you are.
That was—you?
Are you telling me you are the one responsible for that—that—mauling?
It's—the Devil's work. It must be!
Guh—Get away from me! From all of us!
I don't need to reach you. I can kill you with a single word. I have a power—
And—I want this investigated at once. I want to know exactly what took place.
You know, when my father died it felt the same way. I expected sorrow. But—nothing. Just nothing.
Let—Let us speak of that no more, Ophelia. Let it accumulate yesterdays upon its grave.
Don't take this the wrong way, but—what if Hamlet and I began seeing each other again?
That's not a sonnet at all. Fourteen lines of ten syllables—isn't that how it goes?
I—I must admit it has been described to me as a fault of mine.
She's—well, she and Hamlet—
I—I feel exhausted.
And Hamlet's gone now, and, well—
I've witnessed destruction wrought by the very stars themselves, which I thought once were mere fixed illusion—until I'd been to them.
We traveled for two days until we reached the outer limits of Denmark's borders—a small castle of no repute, crumbling away into snow and dirt.
Norway is deflected successfully. But not forever. Fortinbras must be returned to his people, and returned he is—for a price.
But—what I did—it was the best choice, was it not?
Ferdinand assures me that Kalmar is not so different—another country, yes, but very alike. And so we pack our things, and one month after our wedding day, we set forth.
It rarely seems to sputter out entirely—Irma is always working.
She's been through this before. She must know the way out of it all. And—and if this is right, she's still alive!
Let me see if I can find what Claudius asked Bernardo to hide.—Ah. This must be it.
I'm sorry, Father. I don't feel well. I had such an odd vision last night—
Be careful, love. That's all I ask. Carrying on like this—it terrifies me. I don't want you hurt.
The more I think on it, the heavier my heart becomes. I—
Things are almost peaceful, here at the start of it all.
It is impossible, yes. It is the rules of the larger game.
I did not give it that name. But it is a game all the same, and you the one forecasted to lose.
Now then. What news do you bring?
Death becomes you.
Be wary of every familiar face.
One of them will betray you.
Would that I could. But I am unable, through no law of my own.
I'm sure you'll find out soon enough.
I see one of your compatriots has had you killed.
Welcome to the ranks of the famous and esteemed. Those who die before their time live on in memory longer.
Though yours is a more heroic fate than dying on your stomach in the garden.
Of course, they will find your waterlogged corpse in the pond and say you drowned...
Leaving out the gash in your neck when they tell the tale.
Because a gash on an innocent maiden defies explanation. Suicide is a story easily told.
Yes. There is. Your killer may be known to you, as mine was.
Who do you trust to help you unmask them?
The hourglass empties. The days have passed.
Less than one cock's crow remains.
I understand now why my son adores you so.
By the by, I've noticed you are free of your assassin, are you not? You have won this battle.
No. Not the war.
Indeed, it appears he has already done so. See for yourself if he speaks true.
Though by what power he does these things, I know not.
Ah. Still living, I see. So you managed to stay your fate.
I'm impressed. But tomorrow, it will save you no more than the others.
It's what the dead do best.
Fortinbras marches even now. Less than a day, Ophelia.
Can you save them from him?
They are tearing each other apart like men on patrol in a starving winter.
It shall not end until Elsinore lies silent.
Now. What news do you bring?
S-Spirit? Do you—are you here?
Indeed. I am that body once called King Hamlet.
In vague silhouettes and shadows. Memory in death is a struggle. It is faint and infrequent.
I recall you were a young girl once. Such a rambunctious child. I knew you then.
Yes. A world now forever locked behind time's barrier.
The desire to see her safe is often the only thing powerful enough to rouse me.
But in this world, she does not even know of my existence. Would that she and I could speak alone just once.
I have only a single selfish request.
But it may be of use to you.
Seek out your father. Watch what he does when he believes he is alone.
My notes—my notes, taken by him, out of love, out of protection—
They contain the terrifying details of my ordeal. Details I cannot recall. Things too hazy to remember fully.
But that ordeal is the reason I still linger, trapped here.
Find the notes, and there may be freedom for us both.
I have witnessed that your father keeps my possessions under most private lock and key.
The key is on his person at all times. Only he may access what is mine.
There are stronger forces than I at work. Even now, I can only hold my form for so long. Everything from before I walked these walls is... distant.
Find those pages. They rest in your father's care. Please.
Did you cause them to happen? Are you some sort of—sorcerer?
A-and—someone's coming to kill me too, aren't they?
It is with my last fragments of will that I appear to you. I do not know how long I can linger.
No, Ophelia. There is no other way.
What he says is true.
I know that now more than ever. The confines surrounding this world are insurmountable.
Ophelia, there will be no way out from this.
That kind of world was never a possible outcome for you, Ophelia.
No such world of eternal bliss exists. For you, or for anyone on earth.
And it never shall.
But there is something even more powerful.
It is the oldest, most primal power of humankind.
The power to choose with kindness and wisdom is the only thing separating human beings from utter darkness.
You have seen the possibilities of this universe. Now it's up to you to envision its fate.
Let me be clear. There is no perfect world to be found.
But the choice between worlds is a power so critical as to be divinely given, is it not? Freedom of will! The first and last gift granted to Eve herself!
Yes... free will is a sword to cut through the darkness. It is a small boat we cling to in this lifelong storm!
In that, Ophelia, is everything. You must choose, and you must then live in the world which comes from it.
You must do the thing you fear most, and move forward rather than back.
You would punish Quince. But you would condemn every human heart in this castle to their fates. You'd abandon them.
I—This is—But there has to be another way! A good way—a best path!
No. Perfection is impossible. No such world could ever exist. Not so long as imperfect human beings fill it.
Use the Book of Fates, Ophelia. Do what I could not.
Refuse to give up!
Not long now...
If only I had known the kind of strength you possess when I was alive, child.
Though your body might be frail, you are brilliant as the sun.
Someday many years hence, let us play a game of chess together sometime.
Or walk amongst those verdant, shimmering gardens I once slept in peacefully...
I... hope it is permissible that I call you a friend in death, though I hardly knew you in life.
I'm certain we'll see one another again.
It is the end.
And I am not afraid.
Indeed. For a small while, the Book of Fates can make even this miracle possible.
Yes. Although death is what I wished for, once—in my heart I've always been uncertain.
This was the fate I brought upon myself by virtue of my inaction, once.
I did not know I had a choice to make at the time. I never found the Book of Fates. But in my heart of hearts, I chose it all the same.
If this is the future you desire, choose it with intent, Ophelia.
Do not shy away from the world, as I did. Go into the darkness with strength. Go with purpose.
That is all.
Ophelia. Cease this.
You cannot stay in this world.
It has lingered long past its due.
This version of Elsinore... is merely a fantasy.
It is a trick invented by your own mind.
This version of events may never come to pass. This is the reality of this world when all illusion is wiped away. You are alone.
In life, I did not fight Insanity. I relinquished myself to her. I was subjugated, consumed, and finally death took me.
Think carefully on whether you wish to do the same.
While you lie in the grip of your delusion, everyone still alive will meet a grisly fate. No amount of dreaming can save them from that.
T-they're all dead—all of them—
But Guilda—pranks aside, your funeral was attended by those who truly love you. Isn't that enough?
Because my father thought, if Claudius were dead—
You have returned.
It is.
Has it?
Or at least, I think—I think I've been gone a long time.
It felt like an instant between the last time I saw you and this awakening, now. I suppose I must have been waiting for you, then.
Evidently so.
My hands—they're so soft!
You look just as you did then.
Glad to see death hasn't sapped you of your steel.
This is the afterwards. Neither Heaven nor Hell. Simply the nothingness in between.
Of course I do. But why would you consider such a thing?
After all this time...
You left that world behind. Why now?
What difference does that make?
Ophelia. Do you know what I would give to have left Elsinore behind in life, even just once?
That chance was stolen from me.
Now you treat it as though it's something easily exchanged. As though you could put your life back on the shelf and choose another.
I know it's painful. I'm sorry to have woken you again. I wanted to let you rest—I didn't know coming back would be like this.
No, no. There is something you do not understand about the threads of fate, I think. They are woven together as one, a transcendent tapestry.
This is not a simple matter of browsing what might have been.
By choosing the world you did, you pulled that world's thread forever. If you choose to return to Elsinore, you cannot return to the path you chose.
Yes. In other words, you will not be able to return to that particular fate.
It is shattered. Gone. And once you set foot back in Elsinore, you will lose all memory of what you chose.
Your time with Grace—the adventures you embarked on—will vanish.
That sacrifice you made for the sake of others will have been meaningless, for there is no such similar path.
Your memory of the time you spent with Laertes and your father, both the good and bad, will vanish.
You will never again have the power to overturn nations at your whim. At least—not in the same way.
You will never again live out the rest of your life at Hamlet's side.
That perfect world you created will shatter. And I will warn you now: No other fate you could choose could possibly live up to its happiness.
You will never again be able to guarantee that everyone in Elsinore survives.
You will forego the life you and Othello built together. And without leaving Elsinore with you, he is likely to be killed here.
You will never again have a future you built away from Elsinore, on your own, free of others' misery.
Never again will you settle down with Lady Guildenstern and Lady Rosencrantz, though you had found peace with them.
There is no other world with such a peaceful existence for Elsinore as the one where Fortinbras was its true King.
Please. I urge you not to do this, Ophelia. I urge you with everything in my heart.
It's not too late to turn back!
Here you are yet again.
Perhaps. Perhaps not.
What do you recall?
Only that I came here at the end of my life. And I know now—though I did not know in Elsinore—that you and I have spoken here before, in this place.
And what before that? What before we last spoke?
Then it is as I warned you. You have no memory of the fate you chose before.
You already have.
Yes. Your return on that occasion brought you no more happiness than your first fate.
What leads you to believe that this attempt shall yield more fruitful results?
Besides, if you return to Elsinore again, you will lose all memory of this fate, too.
This past time... when you chose your fate... that me, that Hamlet, had no knowledge of this in-between place. Neither did you.
That version of me believed we were still friends. But now, looking at you, my wits about me, I am not so certain.
You need not continue, you know. Will you finally allow all of us to rest?
Or will you force the both of us to continue to endure this hell?
I had thought you'd surely not return.
You know, I cherish you dearly when I am pulled back to Elsinore.
I have no memory of this place, this in-between.
Then I am brought back here when you die, and I remember you chose to return me to Elsinore too, and it aches so terribly.
And this is the third time.
Say, Hamlet—what were those other fates I chose?
Were they—was I—happier?
I suspected you would find yourself wondering this.
But I do not know. I do not see your life beyond Elsinore. I am not a god. Just a man, or what was once a man, standing here as confused as you.
Do not return to Elsinore again.
If ever you did love me, if ever you did find me worthy of your time... then you will join me here in the quiet of oblivion, and take up an eternal rest.
It will never be complete.
I urge you to understand this!
I harbored a deep and impenetrable respect for you in life, Ophelia. Do not prove me a fool in death.
Do not show me that everything we went through together was trivial compared to your pining for the impossible.
If you return to Elsinore again, you will again lose all memory of the fate you just chose, and you will not be able to choose it again. In other words...
You are no better than him, you know.
You have shown me already that, like him, you will not grant mercy.
We are simply playthings to you.
I must remind you, as you abandon the fate you last chose...
Let me give you what you desire, then. The chance to find something else. Something 'better.'
Let me give you what you came here for. We have nothing more to say to one another, after all.
I never thought you were quite this stubborn in life.
Nevertheless, I will show you the way back to Elsinore.
You have my eternal thanks.
You are wiser and more merciful than that broken world ever deserved.
Let us go away now, Ophelia. Forever.
So be it, then.
I mourn the fate you leave behind, for certainly neither you nor I will recall it if we ever meet again.
So be it. I hope we never meet again, then.
And if we ever do, I shall no longer try to stand in your way.
Trying to save someone from pain is a courtesy one only extends to friends.
Indeed. It is possible, though difficult, for me to manifest.
I find it most curious that you are still here.
At the end of the last cycle Fortinbras was rebuked. Was he not?
A natural assumption, of course. And yet, here you are, and here I am, trapped under the lip of the goblet still.
There exist certain undiscovered elements of this world.
Would that I could tell you. These lips are sealed with a far more gruesome power than death.
But that information, created when I still lived, sleeps inside the castle's walls...
In plain sight of all, and accessible to those curious enough to find it.
What... What just—
